content.text: I reviewed the three cases against the claim as written, the quoted source text, and the rubric's counting rules.

findings: Oracle fitness and independence: the keys come from two retrieved public sources — the ChEMBL Interface Documentation ("-Log(molar IC50, XC50, EC50, AC50, Ki, Kd or Potency)"; "an IC50 measurement of 1nM would have a pChEMBL value of 9") and Papadatos et al. 2015 ("the negative logarithm of the activity values (in M units)"). Neither was written by the submitted skill or the verifier, and for a definitional arithmetic claim a major public bioactivity database's published definition plus a peer-reviewed description of its computation is fit for purpose. Two real weaknesses, both disclosed: the sources are both EMBL-EBI products describing one database field, so their agreement is partial corroboration rather than two independent authorities, and neither uses the literal token pIC50 — the identification of pIC50 with the IC50 instance of pChEMBL is asserted by the design, not quoted. For this transform that identification is uncontroversial, so it does not sink the oracle.

Coverage of the stated facts: (a) negation of the logarithm — tested by pic50-transform-shape (distractor 5 drops the negation) and by pic50-one-nanomolar (a sign error gives -9); (b) base 10 rather than natural log — tested by pic50-one-nanomolar (natural log gives ~20.7) and by pic50-transform-shape (distractor 3); (c) IC50 must be in molar units before the transform — tested by pic50-required-units and by pic50-one-nanomolar (logging the bare nanomolar number gives 0). No fact in the statement or expected behaviour is untested, so there are no coverage gaps; python_checked.search_record shows no recorded search, but nothing is left unsourced that a search would need to cover. Coverage is nonetheless thin in depth: a single worked conversion at one magnitude, three trials each, and two of three cases recognition — materially limited coverage, which is exactly what B describes.

Comparison rule and tolerance: the open case is numeric against an exact integer 9 with tolerance 1e-6, which absorbs only formatting (9 vs 9.0); the value is definitional and carries no experimental error, so a measurement-style tolerance would be wrong here and is correctly avoided. The two choice cases are scored as an exact option index. The uncertainty statement is candid about the single magnitude probed, the recognition-heavy mix, the shared EMBL-EBI provenance, and the fact that the design sits at the minimum case count with no spare.

A stronger grade was considered and correctly rejected: A requires at least five counting cases with at least two generated, and this design has three with one generated, so it misses on both counts regardless of oracle quality. The justification's account of why further open cases were not built is honest — the sources carry one worked conversion, the inverse direction is the same rule read backwards, and the only other open token would test a database column name rather than the arithmetic. B is the ceiling the design supports and the ceiling Python computed.
No prior objections were supplied, so there is nothing to verdict.

Each case stays inside the claim. pic50-one-nanomolar applies the whole definition end to end and is generated, so no option can be recognised. pic50-required-units isolates the unit requirement the claim's statement explicitly carries; the word 'molar' is absent from the stem and the three prefixed molar units are the realistic errors, so it is not leaked. pic50-transform-shape isolates the functional form with every option in the same 'the X of the activity values' frame, so there is no style leak. None of the three asks what a higher or lower pIC50 implies about potency, or how pIC50 relates to Ki or EC50, which the claim never states. The two choice cases isolate complementary halves of the composite open case rather than repeating it, so neither is a duplicate.
objections: pic50-required-units states the transform shape in its own stem ("Before the negative base-10 logarithm is taken to give pIC50"), which is precisely the fact pic50-transform-shape asks the subject to recognise. If the cases are ever presented in a shared context or transcript, case 3 is leaked by case 2's wording. Scored as independent prompts the two are clean, so this bears on how the design must be run rather than on whether case 3 counts.

The key of pic50-transform-shape, "the negative logarithm of the activity values", does not state the base, while the claim asserts base 10 specifically. The case therefore confirms a weaker proposition than the claim; the base is only pinned by pic50-one-nanomolar. This limits the case's strength but does not make another option, including 'none of these', as defensible as the key, since option 2 is consistent with the claim and every alternative contradicts it.

Because the design holds exactly three counting cases with exactly one generated, it has no margin: were either choice case judged unfit, the design would fall below B and below C. The uncertainty note acknowledges this, but it remains a structural fragility of the evidence rather than a disclosed limitation that is thereby cured.

pic50-one-nanomolar.reason: Generated numeric case applying the full definition: the subject must read 1 nM as 1e-9 M and take the negative base-10 logarithm. Errors on either half produce distinct wrong answers (0 for logging the bare nanomolar figure, ~20.7 for natural logs, -9 for a sign error), the expected value 9 is quoted verbatim from the ChEMBL documentation, and nothing in the stem reveals it.

pic50-required-units.reason: The claim's statement explicitly requires IC50 in molar units, so this tests a fact the claim asserts and no more. The word 'molar' does not appear in the stem, the distractors are the prefixed units that real bioactivity tables actually store, and no option repeats question wording, so the key cannot be recovered without the claim. It isolates one half of the composite open case rather than repeating it, so it is not a duplicate.

pic50-transform-shape.reason: Tests the functional form the claim asserts — negation applied to a logarithm — with distractors that drop the negation, change the base, or substitute another function, and with no mention of units so it cannot be answered from the unit fact. The key is quoted verbatim from the peer-reviewed source and every option shares the same grammatical frame. Its omission of the base makes it a weaker test than the claim's full statement, but no alternative option is as defensible as the key.
